title: It is important to remember that investors do care about affordability. In fact, the affordability crisis is why Fitch downgraded the outlook for US utilities to “deteriorating.” Which makes sense… | Joseph Daniel
description:
It is important to remember that investors do care about affordability. In fact, the affordability crisis is why Fitch downgraded the outlook for US utilities to “deteriorating.” Which makes sense. How can a utility reasonably be expected to recover its costs if its customers can't afford to pay their electric bill? 

But utilities aren't helpless. Here are three things I think investors should be pushing that will help:

1. Target customer affordability programs
If customers can pay their bills, that improves utility cash flow and reduces bad debt. Programs that target customers at risk of falling behind deliver more benefits per dollar than broad-based approaches. This includes taking action to improve adoption of these policies; the more customers that take advantage of them, the more benefits they will produce. 

2. Get smarter about cost allocation.
Most people think of cost allocation as simply dividing up the pie of a utility's costs. But it is more than just distribution. When done properly, it can put downward pressure on long-run costs. The way costs are allocated creates price signals that can change customer behavior (which in turn affects utility investment decisions). Probability-of-dispatch, hourly cost modeling, and other more sophisticated methods can better align prices with the costs customers actually impose on the system and avoid incentives that drive up long-run costs.

3. Create customer subclasses when customers have fundamentally different needs.
Data centers want speed-to-power and have a high willingness to pay (are less price sensitive). Low-income customers are already struggling and are very price sensitive. Fixed-income customers are price sensitive, but they are even more sensitive to volatility. Creating appropriate subclasses can allow utilities and regulators to design tariffs and programs around those differences, while protecting other customers from paying for costs they don't cause.

There are a lot more things utilities can be doing, and the investor community should be pressuring them to be proactive in addressing these problems. 

What do you think? What other things can utilities do that will improve affordability and their bottom line?

name: Affordability Crisis
title: Ivana (@ivanaunfiltered)
description:
New York Has Finally Solved the Affordability Crisis

Manhattan’s average asking rent has reached $6,655amonth.

That is $79,860 a year.

Not to own anything.

Not to build equity.

Not even to discover, after thirty years, that there is perhaps a small patch of earth somewhere in Queens with your name on it.

No.

That is approximately eighty thousand dollars a year for the privilege of giving somebody else eighty thousand dollars a year.

Welcome to New York.

But Don’t Worry. The Socialists Are Here.

Naturally, when confronted with a housing market requiring the annual income of a minor European principality to rent a two-bedroom apartment, New Yorkers decided what they really needed was more government involvement.

And so Mayor Zohran Mamdani came to the rescue.

The Rent Guidelines Board has approved a rent freeze for rent-stabilized apartments beginning this fall.

Because if there is one thing everybody remembers from Economics 101, it is:

When something is scarce, make absolutely certain there is no additional incentive to supply it.

I believe that was somewhere between supply and demand and the chapter titled Fuck Around and Find Out.

A Brief Economics Lesson

Here is the boring capitalist version.

If lots of people want apartments and there are not enough apartments, apartments become expensive.

Very complicated.

Economists have been studying this mysterious phenomenon for several centuries.

The traditional solution is to make it easier, faster and more profitable to create more apartments.

More supply.

More competition.

More choices for renters.

Eventually, less ability for a landlord to look you directly in the eye and ask $4,000 a month for a studio containing one window, half a radiator and what the listing describes as “European charm.”

The political solution is more exciting.

Control the price.

Tax another thing.

Regulate another thing.

Create another board.

Hold a press conference.

Blame capitalism.

Repeat until Brooklyn requires a hedge fund to qualify as a guarantor.

And Then Came the Grocery Stores

Housing is not the only thing New York has decided the government might like to sell you.

The Mamdani administration is putting $70 million toward five municipal grocery stores — one in each borough.

Yes.

Government grocery stores.

We have arrived.

Your rent is $6,655.

Your taxes are enormous.

Your corner grocery is struggling with enormous rent, labor costs, insurance, utilities, regulations and approximately seventeen thousand other expenses involved in operating a business in New York City.

So naturally the government looked at that businessman and said:

Have you considered competing against us? We have taxpayer money.

Beautiful.

Absolutely beautiful.

The Department of Avocados

And listen, I understand why this stuff sells politically.

People are hurting.

When somebody is choosing between groceries and rent, “we will make your groceries cheaper” sounds considerably more appealing than a forty-minute explanation involving zoning, construction costs, permitting, incentives, tax policy and housing supply.

That is how populism works.

It offers you an immediate villain and an immediate present.

Landlord bad.

Corporation bad.

Profit bad.

Here is cheaper milk.

Please do not inspect the machinery behind the curtain.

But somebody always pays.

There is no enchanted municipal cow producing government milk behind City Hall.

There is no secret warehouse of socialist tomatoes waiting to be liberated from capitalism.

There are taxpayers.

There are subsidies.

There are costs.

There are consequences.

And eventually there is a government employee explaining why Form GR-17B must be completed before you may purchase the reasonably priced zucchini.

New Yorkers Have Seen This Movie Before

This is what makes the whole thing particularly hilarious to me.

New York is already one of the most taxed, regulated, controlled, bureaucratic places in America.

It has rules for the rules.

It has departments supervising departments.

Somewhere in lower Manhattan there is probably a Deputy Assistant Commissioner for Reviewing the Committee That Reviews Things.

And after decades of making it extraordinarily expensive to live, build and operate a business here, the political conclusion is apparently:

We have not governmented hard enough.

That’s the diagnosis.

More.

More intervention.

More controls.

More public programs.

More taxes to pay for the programs designed to make affordable the things that became unaffordable while we were taxing and regulating them.

At this rate, by 2028 every New Yorker will receive three subsidized onions, a MetroCard and a pamphlet explaining why capitalism did this.

Meanwhile, Back in Manhattan

Average asking rent:

$6,655.

A month.

And somehow an entire city looked at that number and thought:

You know what we should try?

Socialism.

Godspeed, New York.

I’ll see you in line at the Department of Avocados.

Ivana 🗽
